messages.subject: Is there a way to get sjp.lmer type graphs or plots like marginal effects plots for random factors?
messages.subject_clean: Is there a way to get sjp.lmer type graphs or plots like marginal effects plots for random factors?
messages.body_plain:
The graphs I'm referencing are here <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/sjPlot/vignettes/sjplmer.html>, namely, the ones towards the bottoms with random slopes and random intercepts.

Basically, what I am trying to do is get plots of the relationship between a predictor variable and the outcome variable across different levels of a random effect (institutions). I also have a fixed effect, Sex.

The model is of the form

y ~ b1:fixed + b2:fixed + (1|random)

I chose the form b1:fixed rather than b1*fixed because I don't care about the influence of sex as such on predicting the outcome variable, only how sex affects the influence b1 and b2 have on y. Getting the marginal effects is easy for the fixed effects with the marginal_effects function, but I'd like to see how this varies across the locations data were collected.

I used the LibreOffice template by Rasmus Bååth for a first sketch but I'm unsure if I'm correctly visualizing the zero-inflation and the beta part of the model. In case there's someone with more experience on how to visualize complex probabilistic models, I would highly appreciate some input or ideas on how to best display the zero_inflated_beta model in such a diagram.

Here's some example code and the diagram:

# y_beta is beta distributed with some 0s
# x1, x2 are normaly distributed
# x2, x3, x4, x5, x6 are binary coded with 0/1
# model uses default priors (half student-t)
brm(bf(y_beta ~ x1+ x2 + x3, zi ~ x1 + x4 + x5 + x6), data, family = zero_inflated_beta)

Thanks!

messages.subject: Specifying cumulative ordinal model with two factors
messages.subject_clean: Specifying cumulative ordinal model with two factors
messages.body_plain:
Hello all.

I'm trying to specify a cumulative ordinal regression. I had people rate images with two factors, each with three levels (the same levels). The images had two dimensions, *relevant* and *incidental*. Each of these has three levels: modal, extreme, and marginal. People rated how typical each image was on a scale from 1 to 7.

What I'm trying to figure out to specify and interpret a model around this. And I get different results depending on how I specify it. Part of this stems from my confusion about what contrasts to specify. On twitter, Paul said that I should use dummy or effects coding for each predictor. In this situation, I'm not sure what the predictor should be.

I've specified one model,

rf1.full <- brm(c_rating ~ label_relevant * label_incidental + (label_relevant * label_incidental | uniqueid), data = d, family = cumulative)

Where c_rating is an ordered factor from 1 to 7, label_relevant and label_incidental are factors with three level, of which mode is the reference level. When I examine the plots from `marginal_effects` the graphs make sense and show two factors with three levels each. I can interpret these, I think. What doesn't make sense is that the factors in the output of `summary` are just labelled "label_relevant1" and "label_relevant2", and "label_incidental1_ and "label_incidental2". I'm pretty sure these track the same levels as in the factor (in that the intercept is the mode, level 1 is extreme, level 2 is marginal). But I'm not sure and I'm not sure how to check what's what.

But the other way he could've meant is to specify a model such as this (interaction between the factors isn't a thing, really):

rf2.full <- brm(c_rating ~ labRel_Marginal + labRel_Extreme + labInc_Marginal + labInc_Extreme + (labRel_Marginal + labRel_Extreme + labInc_Marginal + labInc_Extreme | uniqueid), data = d, family = cumulative)
Where each level is dummy-coded. I find it a lot harder to interpret this.

ALSO: I'm also struggling how to specify contrasts. So far, because I mostly work with ANOVAs, I've specified the factors' contrast levels in the first example as `contr.sum`. But I'm not sure how to interpret those results very easily, so I've also done it with contr.treatment and it makes more sense (and corresponds to the graphs in maringal_effects).

Really, I think I'm just asking what the norm is for specifying this kind of model with this kind of question. Any guidance is helpful. I am but a rowboat adrift in the sea.

messages.body_plain:
Yes, certainly, sorry.

This would be a model for fMRI data. The basic model is:

y ~ (X * h(theta)) B

y are a continuous-valued data (n x 1 vector). X is an (n x m) design matrix of zeros and ones, in which there are m different kind of stimulus conditions. The * is meant to represent column-wise convolution with the response function h(theta). theta are the parameters of the response function, and while it would be awesome to estimate them they are almost always just fixed. B is the m x 1 vector of parameter values to estimate.

The scenario is that a person goes in to an fMRI scanner and is presented with different kinds of visual stimuli. Measurements are collected about once every 2 seconds, corresponding to their brain's current activity at that time (which is partitioned into a collection of 3x3x3 mm 'voxels'). The brain's response to a stimulus usually lasts a bit, first dipping below baseline then rising then falling back below baseline then returning to baseline. The entire response takes about 20 seconds (the measurement is actually a measurement of blood flow). It's lasting response that is modeled by h(). That response function is roughly linear with respect to the design matrix, in that presentation for a stimulus for 4 seconds is expected to produce a response that is about twice as much as a 2 second stimulus. The interpretation of B is then the amplitude of the response function (how much the brain responds to a particular kind of stimulus).
     There are other components that make things more complex quickly, including auto-regressive noise, regressors dealing with nuisance factors (e.g., breathing or heart rate), heirarchies placed on B. But, my main question was just about whether it was possible to incorporate the X * h() part.

Perhaps I'm doing something wrong in processing the predictions?

messages.subject_clean: [brms-users] "acat" and "cumulative" outputting different predictions?
messages.body_plain:
Sure. This is kind of a janky way of simulating the data but it illustrates the problem:

##### simulate

set.seed(1)
# the majority of outcomes are category "1"
ordered_outcome <- c(rep(1,300),rep(2,150),rep(3,75))
measure_subscale <- c(rep(1,100),rep(2,100),rep(3,100),
                      rep(1,50),rep(2,50),rep(3,50),
                      rep(1,25),rep(2,25),rep(3,25))
# crude way of simulating a relationship between subscales and outcome
score <- rnorm(length(ordered_outcome), ordered_outcome * measure_subscale, .5)
ordered_outcome <- as.ordered(ordered_outcome)
measure_subscale <- factor(measure_subscale, levels=1:3, labels=c("A", "B", "C"))
dt.lng <- data.frame(ordered_outcome, measure_subscale, score)

## Draw a histogram of the density of scores on each measure subscale by outcome
densplot <- dt.lng %>%
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = score, fill=ordered_outcome) +
  geom_density(show.legend = T) +
  xlab("score on subscales A, B, and C") + ylab("frequency")
densplot + facet_wrap(~measure_subscale)

cumulative_model <- brm(ordered_outcome ~ score + (1 + score | measure_subscale),
             data = dt.lng, iter=500, cores=4, chains=4, family="cumulative")
cumulative_predictions <- predict(cumulative_model) # get predictions for the input data
cumulative_predictions <- apply(cumulative_predictions,1,which.max) # get category with the highest probability for each case
dt.lng <- cbind(dt.lng, cumulative_predictions)

p <- ggplot(dt.lng) +
  aes(x = cumulative_predictions, y = ordered_outcome, col=score) +
  geom_jitter(height=.1,width=.1,alpha=.6) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low="blue", high="red") +
  ylab("Outcome; as observed") +
  labs(col="Observed\nscore", title="family=cumulative (this model looks appropriate)") +
  xlab("Outcome; as predicted")
p + facet_wrap(~measure_subscale)

acat_model <- brm(ordered_outcome ~ score + (1 + score | measure_subscale),
                        data = dt.lng, iter=500, cores=4, chains=4, family="acat")
acat_predictions <- predict(acat_model) # get predictions for the input data
acat_predictions <- apply(acat_predictions,1,which.max) # get category with the highest probability for each case
dt.lng <- cbind(dt.lng, acat_predictions)

p <- ggplot(dt.lng) +
  aes(x = acat_predictions, y = ordered_outcome, col=score) +
  geom_jitter(height=.1,width=.1,alpha=.6) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low="blue", high="red") +
  ylab("Outcome; as observed") +
  labs(col="Observed\nscore", labs="family=acat (this doesn't look right)") +
  xlab("Outcome; as predicted")
p + facet_wrap(~measure_subscale)

# everyone gets predicted level "3"
# in my 'real' dataset there is some variation in predictions (not everyone
# is predicted to fall into the same category) but the predictions are about
# as unreasonable
table(dt.lng$acat_predictions)

messages.body_plain:
With regard to predictions and model fit, they are usually very similar. The main difference is their theoretical derivation.

The cumulative model assumes a continuous latent process that produces the observered categories through categorization.

The sequential model(s) assummes a sequential process the in the end provided the obserserved categories.

The adjacent category model has (in my opinion) no such derivation and is usually used for mathematical convenience,

Here is what I write about them in some of my workshop slides:

## Which Ordinal Model Should I Use?

Is the assumption of a latent continuous variable plausible?

- If yes: use the cumulative model

Is the assumption of a sequential process plausible?

- If yes: use the sequential model

Does sampling speed matter?

- If yes: use the cumulative model

Do I want to model category specific effects?

- If yes: do not use the cumulative model

That response function is roughly linear with respect to the design matrix, in that presentation for a stimulus for 4 seconds is expected to produce a response that is about twice as much as a 2 second stimulus. As the models take some time to run and I had issues with divergent transitions (note the high adapt_delta values below), I've also shared the two models (brms.rdata <https://drive.google.com/file/d/13UiGIqJxuTDHqJRh6B-no0E-l5aqsr7W/view?usp=sharing>; rstanarm.rdata <https://drive.google.com/file/d/1qGYQOWb6zNaUDJbRzEsEan_YD35GSlRx/view?usp=sharing>).

The code used to fit the models is as follows:

library(rstanarm)
library(brms)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

testing_data <- read.csv('testing_data.csv')

p <- c(set_prior('normal(2,2)', class='Intercept', coef=''),
       set_prior('normal(0,1)', class='b'))

m.brm <- brm(gpa ~ Condition*Ethnicity + (1|ID) +
               (Condition*Ethnicity|site), data=testing_data,
             control=list(adapt_delta=.9999, max_treedepth=15), prior=p)
m.rstanarm <- stan_glmer(gpa ~ Condition*Ethnicity + (1|ID) +
                           (Condition*Ethnicity|site),
                         prior_intercept=normal(2,2), prior=normal(0,1),
                         data=testing_data, adapt_delta = .9999999)

Thanks Travis for providing such detailed information.
The posterior-mean values of the random effects SDs of site appear to be larger in brms:

> VarCorr(m.brm)$site$sd[, "Estimate", drop = FALSE]
                                   Estimate
Intercept                         0.4496999
ConditionTreatment                0.3888073
EthnicityWhite                    0.4617288
ConditionTreatment:EthnicityWhite 0.5834659

than in rstanarm:

> VarCorr(m.rstanarm)
 Groups   Name                              Std.Dev. Corr
 ID       (Intercept)                       0.75533
 site     (Intercept)                       0.27836
          ConditionTreatment                0.22673  -0.097
          EthnicityWhite                    0.23986   0.085 -0.099
          ConditionTreatment:EthnicityWhite 0.25943   0.033 -0.083 -0.184
 Residual                                   0.44043

I have to investigate this in more detail, but this might be the result of narrower priors on the group-level SDs of site in rstanarm as compared to brms. Since larger values of the group-level SDs imply larger variation in the population-level effects, this might explain the differences you observed.

In contrast, the SD of ID and the residual SD is pretty similar for both packages since in brms:

> VarCorr(m.brm)$ID$sd[, "Estimate"]
[1] 0.7569105
> VarCorr(m.brm)$residual__$sd[, "Estimate"]
[1] 0.4405743

similar to what we see above from rstanarm. Accordingly I would expect this to be a problem of too narrow priors of the SDs in rstanarm, but only for correlated group-level effects. Again, this conclusion is preliminary and needs to be investigated further also by the Stan Team.

Thanks Travis for providing such detailed information.
The posterior-mean values of the random effects SDs of site appear to be larger in brms:

> VarCorr(m.brm)$site$sd[, "Estimate", drop = FALSE]
                                   Estimate
Intercept                         0.4496999
ConditionTreatment                0.3888073
EthnicityWhite                    0.4617288
ConditionTreatment:EthnicityWhite 0.5834659

than in rstanarm:

> VarCorr(m.rstanarm)
 Groups   Name                              Std.Dev. Corr
 ID       (Intercept)                       0.75533
 site     (Intercept)                       0.27836
          ConditionTreatment                0.22673  -0.097
          EthnicityWhite                    0.23986   0.085 -0.099
          ConditionTreatment:EthnicityWhite 0.25943   0.033 -0.083 -0.184
 Residual                                   0.44043

I have to investigate this in more detail, but this might be the result of narrower priors on the group-level SDs of site in rstanarm as compared to brms. Since larger values of the group-level SDs imply larger variation in the population-level effects, this might explain the differences you observed.

In contrast, the SD of ID and the residual SD is pretty similar for both packages since in brms:

> VarCorr(m.brm)$ID$sd[, "Estimate"]
[1] 0.7569105
> VarCorr(m.brm)$residual__$sd[, "Estimate"]
[1] 0.4405743

similar to what we see above from rstanarm. Accordingly I would expect this to be a problem of too narrow priors of the SDs in rstanarm, but only for correlated group-level effects. Again, this conclusion is preliminary and needs to be investigated further also by the Stan Team.

target += student_t_lpdf(sd_2 | 3, 0, 10)
    - 5 * student_t_lccdf(0 | 3, 0, 10);

messages.subject_clean: Evidence Ratio for Stanreg objects, and influence by priors
messages.body_plain:
Dear Paul,
Hope that my message finds you well.

I am a cognitive psychologist analyzing the data of psychophysical experiments in multilevel regression models. I ran my models in RStanArm, and currently writing my results in a paper.

I came across your "hypothesis" function and applied it to the Stanreg object.

Does the function take into account the prior distribution I defined for the coefficient in RStanArm? It seems that the function was able to perform a one-sided(a>b), but not two-sided(a=b), hypothesis test. In the latter, I got "NA" as the Evid. Ratio.
When I ran the same model using the brm function with the argument sample_prior= TRUE, I was able to do the two-sided test.

Is there a way to do the two-sided test for existing Stanreg objects as well?

In addition, what is your opinion regarding the strong influence of the prior on the Evidence Ratio? with priors of normal(0,2) or normal(0,10) for the coeffs, I observed Evidence Ratio of ~13 and ~58, accordingly.

Thanks for the help, and lots of gratitude for creating this wonderful package,

Dan

messages.body_plain:
As explained in ?hypothesis, The evidence ratio of a>b is the ratio of posterior probabilities, while a = b is a bayes factor computed via a savage-dickey ratio.

The latter requires samples of the prior distribution, which a stanreg object does not contain. So for a = b, the evid ratio will always be NA for stanreg objects.

Since the evidence ratio of a = b is a bayes factor it will be definition be strongly influenced by the prior (see basically every paper about BFs).
This is one reason I am not a fan of BFs since they depend so critically of the prior.

messages.body_plain:
I have teens and adults in my data set, and wish to test a hypothesis that the influence of a brain region  on a personality trait is greater in teens than it is in adults. The adults are the dummy factor.

Does it make sense to compare the coefficient of the interaction to the main effect directly? (A)  Or should I account for the intercept and main effect of age? (B)

(A) hypothesis(MODEL, "AGE_GROUPTEEN:node_275  > node_275", alpha = .10)

(B) hypothesis(MODEL, "AGE_GROUPTEEN:node_275 + AGE_GROUPTEEN + Intercept  > node_275 + Intercept", alpha = .10)

I am thinking probably A, but interactions can be a little tricky to think about.
